_note: Input to tools/build-sentences.mjs.
The target words are not listed here. They are read out of the already
generated data/vocab/<file>, so a chapter's example sentences can only ever
contain words that chapter teaches. Listing them twice would let the two
files disagree, and the symptom would be an example sentence for a word the
learner has not met.
Run tools/build-vocab.mjs first. build-sentences.mjs says so and stops if
the slice is not there.
`per_word` is 1 in the two newest slices on purpose. A choice round whose
prompt is the word and whose answer is the whole sentence draws its wrong
options from the sibling sentences, so a second sentence for the same word
is a second right answer: asked which sentence uses ようこそ, the learner
sees two that do and is marked wrong for picking either one.
`pins` names a Tatoeba Japanese id for one word id of the slice's vocabulary
file, and it is checked against the pool rather than trusted: an id that no
longer resolves stops the run. It exists because the automatic search is a
substring test on the dictionary form, which has no word boundary to work
with: it matched an adverb for the humble verb of saying and a noun for the
humble verb of doing, and it found nothing at all for the honorific verb of
looking and the humble verb of knowing, because those appear in the corpus
only conjugated. Where a pin is set, the search does not run for that word.

title.en: The phrase in a real sentence
title.es: La frase en una oración real

slices.pins_note: w_0007 is the expression for leaving before the others. The automatic pick was the one sentence in the corpus that uses it the other way round, waving somebody else through a door, which is the opposite of the move the rung teaches. The pinned line is the one every office says at the end of the day.

title.es: El registro en una oración real

slices.pins_note: Six of the eighteen register verbs. Two were matched by substring to a sentence that does not contain them at all, two had no sentence of any kind because they never appear unconjugated, and two had one that is a poor model for a politeness chapter: an archaic imperative and a piece of rude slang. Each pin is a short, ordinary, polite line that uses the verb the way the rung describes.
